chunks: Abd al-Wahid ibn Muhammad ibn Abdus al-Attar al-Naysaburi told us, saying: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Qutaybah narrated to us, from Hamman ibn Sulayman, from Abd al-Salam ibn Salih al-Harawi, who said: I said to al-Rida (peace be upon him):

O son of the Messenger of God, it has been narrated from your fathers (peace be upon them) that for one who has intercourse in the month of Ramadan or breaks his fast in it, there are three expiations. And it has also been narrated from them that there is only one expiation. So which of the two reports should we follow?

He said: We take both. Whenever a man has intercourse in a state of prohibition (or breaks his fast in a state of prohibition) in the month of Ramadan, he is obligated to three expiations: freeing a slave, fasting two consecutive months, and feeding sixty poor people, plus making up that day's fast.
And if he married (or broke his fast) in a permissible state, he is obligated to one expiation and making up that day's fast. And if he was forgetful, there is no expiation upon him.

key_terms.كفارة: Expiation or compensation for a religious violation

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the three expiations and the single expiation for breaking the fast in Ramadan according to Imam al-Rida?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Ma'ani al-Akhbar*, Imam al-Rida (AS) harmonizes conflicting reports by distinguishing between the legal status of the act itself rather than merely the intent. He establishes that a 'prohibited' act (haram) incurs three cumulative expiations—freeing a slave, fasting two consecutive months, and feeding sixty poor—alongside making up the day, whereas a 'permissible' act (halal) requires only one expiation and making up the day. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance that the severity of the penalty correlates with the intrinsic prohibition of the act performed during the sacred month.
